newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian farmers urge native title changes.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian farmers urge native title changes.

text.p: Australia's peak farm body, the National Farmers' Federation, said on Friday it would strongly press Prime Minister John Howard to legislate to give pastoralists exclusive occupancy on their leases.
NFF president Donald McGauchie told reporters ahead of a meeting with Howard that the conflict between native title and pastoralists' rights would cost Australia dearly if not quickly resolved.
McGauchie said mining output would be affected before farm output, but that already farming activities were beginning to be affected.
McGauchie strongly criticised the High Court for determining in a split decision that pastoral leases did not automatically extinguish native title.
The High Court ruling in December found that Aboriginal native title and pastoral leases could co-exist.

Warning that the native title conflict would be "enormously expensive" for Australia, McGauchie said he would call on Howard to legislate to ensure the validation of all acts in relation to freehold, residential, commercial and agricultural leases, and public works.
The NFF was also calling for cities, town sites and land and water resouces reserved for public purposes to be quarantined from the future act regime of the Native Title Act.
He described the native title conflict as "one of the most difficult problems this country has ever faced".

"This will be enormously expensive for this country," McGauchie said. "Whatever happens this country is going to lose some of its growth, some of its jobs. It's going to cost us a great deal of money," he said.
McGauchie said a meeting of state farmer organisations this week had agreed to call for undertakings of the former Keating government in 1993 to be honoured.
These meant that the valid grant of a pastoral lease gave exclusive occupancy to the leaseholder, he said.
The High Court's finding had caused confusion and despair among Australia's pastoralists, he said.
Only the government, and not the High Court, had power to produce a reconciliation, he said.
